catalog_quote: 1.2. STRESS. Stress is marked by increased volume, vowel length, and a slight rise in pitch. Primary stress is highly predictable, occurring on the penultimate syllable in all indigenous forms except for a few two-syllable conjunctions, demonstratives, and pronouns in which primary stress is consistently on the ultimate syllable (e.g. [pa.tíʔ] 'and', [ʔa.tó] 'here', and [ka.ʔáw] 'you').3 Some nonassimilated loan words also have ultimate stress. Secondary stress occurs on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end of the word. It is less intense than primary stress, but is discernible in long words as cadence in which every other vowel is slightly longer and louder than the unstressed vowels in between. [ag.pà.malàm.pa.sú.ko] 'I told them to scrub the floor' [ag.pà.ma.líg.ya] 'they are the ones offering for sale', [kì.na.háŋ.lan] 'need'. There is a limited set of one-syllable particles which carry no stress and are not postclitics, e.g. [pa] 'still' and [na] 'already'.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Everything else, including 'Secondary stress occurs on the fourth and sixth syllables…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every native word; a closed list of disyllabic conjunctions, demonstratives and pronouns (pati 'and', ato 'here', ka'aw 'you') and some unassimilated Spanish loans take final stress. Secondary stress alternates leftward from the primary (4th and 6th syllables from the end), giving a trochaic cadence in long words. The domain is the phonological word, which includes proclitic and enclitic particles (sec. 1.1, p. 33; orthography note p. 42); a small set of monosyllabic particles (pa 'still', na 'already') carry no stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress occurs on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end of the word', i.e. on alternate syllables to the left of the penult; less intense than primary, heard as a cadence in long words, e.g. [ag.pà.malàm.pa.sú.ko] 'I told them to scrub the floor', [kì.na.háŋ.lan] 'need' (p. 34).
new_statements.exceptions: Ultimate stress in a few two-syllable conjunctions, demonstratives and pronouns ([pa.tí] 'and', [ʔa.tó] 'here', [ka.ʔáw] 'you') and in some non-assimilated loanwords; footnote 3 (p. 34): the 1sg pronoun /ʔá.ku/ 'I' takes either ultimate or penultimate stress depending on phrase-level intonation, e.g. [ʔá.ko..] vs [.. a.kó..]; 'Similar stress variation has not been noted with other pronouns.' Monosyllabic particles [pa] 'still', [na] 'already' carry no stress. The Spanish-loan subsystem is treated separately: loans keep their own (sometimes final) stress; vowel allophony rules (sec. 4.4.2, p. 39) are keyed to the 'stressed syllable (usually penultimate)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'A phonological word consists of one or more syllables, with word juncture marked by the stress pattern' (sec. 1.1, p. 33); pre- and postclitic particles count as part of the phonological word for stress and vowel-variant purposes (p. 42). Data collected April-November 1979 on Capul Island, Northern Samar (fn. 1, p. 32). The stress claims are impressionistic (SIL tagmemic phonemic statement), not instrumental.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language 'Sama Abaknon'; fn. 1 (p. 32) says native speakers call it Inabaknon and Samar residents call it Capuleño, and that 'Abaknon' is properly the ethnonym ('one who comes from Abak', the pre-Spanish name of Capul Island). Data were collected on Capul Island, Northern Samar, in 1979 from three named native speakers; no dialect split is described. This is the same languoid as Glottolog inab1237 (ISO abx), no separate dialect glottocode needed.

new_statements.quote: [p. 94, sec. 3.5 STRESS] Primary stress in PSB occurs regularly on the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word, reconstructed on the basis of its reflex on the penult in all SB languages except in predictable environments in NB. This observation applies to words, not merely to stems, so that suffixation results in the shift of stress to the right. [p. 164, sec. 5.1.3] Predictable word stress is a feature of all SB daughter languages including AB, despite the latter's long interaction [with] SMR, a Central Philippine language which has contrastive stress. [p. 277, Appendix I] Note that stress in all Sama-Bajaw languages falls on the penult, with rare exceptions which are indicated.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Jacobson & Jacobson 1980: predictable penultimate primary stress): Pallesen states predictable penultimate word stress for all SB languages 'including AB'. Compatible extra detail: the stress domain is the suffixed word (stress shifts right under suffixation, stated for PSB/SB generally with a Central Sama example). Less detail than the catalog source: no secondary stress, no AB-specific exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In all Sama-Bajaw languages, Abaknun (AB = Sama Abaknon) explicitly included, word stress is predictable (non-contrastive) and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the domain is the whole word including suffixes, so suffixation shifts stress rightward to the new penult. Pallesen stresses that AB kept predictable penultimate stress despite long contact with Samarenyo (Waray), which has contrastive stress. The only SB exception he describes is Northern Borneo (NB) Sama (ultima stress when the penult vowel is schwa), not AB; the Appendix I entry for Abaknun flags no exception.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said (no mention of secondary stress anywhere in the text)
new_statements.exceptions: none for AB; for SB generally 'rare exceptions which are indicated' (Appendix I), and the NB schwa-penult -> ultima rule (sec. 3.5), which does not concern Abaknon. Pallesen does not mention the final-stressed disyllabic function words or unassimilated loans that Jacobson & Jacobson 1980 list.
new_statements.identity_note: Pallesen's 'Abaknun (AB)': self-designation Qinabaknun / kinapul, Capul Island off northwest Samar plus settlements on a neighbouring island and one barrio of Allen, Northern Samar; 9-10,000 speakers; his AB data = text (Wolff), small dictionary (Sylvia Manaog), 2,500-word lexicon and grammatical data (Pallesen). This is Glottolog inab1237 Inabaknon / Sama Abaknon [abx]. The stress statements are made for Proto-Sama-Bajaw and all SB daughter languages, with AB named explicitly on p. 164.

new_statements.quote: Stress is never written for Inabaknon, therefore to pronounce the words correctly place stress on the second to the last syllable, as in: ma-HA-lap AL-law (Good day) and RU-ma' (house). One syllable pronouns should be considered as part of the word for pronunciation purposes, thus: ru-MA' ko (my house) and ma-TA mo (your eyes).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate; penultimate stress) and as the existing statement from Jacobson & Jacobson 1980 Sama Abaknon phonology (PJL 11(1), sec. 1.2). Adds one detail not in the catalog record: monosyllabic enclitic pronouns are counted inside the stress domain, so the host word's stress moves to its final syllable before them (ru-MA' ko). Same authors, same year, same fieldwork (Capul Town, April 1980).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not marked in the orthography because it is predictable: it falls on the second-to-last syllable of the word. Monosyllabic (enclitic) pronouns count as part of the word for stress purposes, so stress shifts one syllable to the right before them (RU-ma' 'house' but ru-MA' ko 'my house', ma-TA mo 'your eyes'), i.e. penult of the word-plus-enclitic domain.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (this is a practical pronunciation note in a phrase book preface, not a phonology).
new_statements.exceptions: None listed here; the only special case given is that one-syllable pronouns are included in the stress domain (ru-MA' ko). The final-stressed disyllabic conjunctions/demonstratives/pronouns and unassimilated Spanish loans noted in Jacobson & Jacobson 1980 (PJL 11) are not mentioned in the phrase book.
new_statements.identity_note: The work is explicitly about Sama Abaknon = Inabaknon = Capuleño of Capul Island (San Bernardino Strait, Northern Samar), 'the most northern representative of the Sama Bajaw language family' (Preface p. viii); data checked by native speakers of Capul Town under the Jacobsons, April 1980. The Glottolog citation's '356 pp.' does not match the item's actual extent (xvii+138 pp., 156-page scan); title, compilers, year, publisher and half-title 'Sama Abaknon Phrase Book' (p. ii verso) confirm it is the same work.
